summary: A Zigzag puppy-training blog article by Petrina Firth explaining the anatomy of dog eyes and how puppy eyes develop and work. It covers the parts of the eye, rods and cones, the tapetum lucidum for low-light vision, dichromatic colour vision (blue and yellow), and simple eye care tips, noting that flat-faced breeds like Pugs and French Bulldogs need more eye care. The rest of the page is app promotion, testimonials, and cookie-consent boilerplate.
one_line: A Zigzag puppy-expert article on dog eye anatomy, how puppy eyes develop, dog colour and night vision, and basic eye care.
key_facts: Dog eyes are made up of a cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, and sclera, plus upper, lower and third eyelids.
The cornea is the transparent dome-like structure covering the front of the eye and bends light as it enters.
Cones allow dogs to see colours, while rods allow them to see shapes.
Puppies are born with their eyelids closed because their eyes are not fully developed.
Puppy eyes open around 14 days and usually one at a time.
Puppy eyes reach full development at around 8 weeks of age.
Dogs have dichromatic vision and only see blue/yellow, plus shades of grey and brown.
Dogs have only around 20% of the cones that humans do.
The tapetum lucidum is a reflective system behind the retina that enhances visual sensitivity at low light levels.
Dogs' wild ancestors were crepuscular, meaning they hunted at dawn and dusk.
Dogs have three eyelids; the third eyelid sweeps back and forth to spread tear film and keep the eye moisturised.
Puppy eyes should be cleaned with cooled boiled water on a cotton pad; harsh chemicals are not needed.
If a dog's eyes are runny, inflamed or bloodshot, owners should see a vet instead of diagnosing at home with eye drops.
Pugs and French Bulldogs need more eye care due to their flat faces, higher risk of gunk, and cherry eye and ulcers.
Blue and yellow toys are best because dogs can find and see them easily.
